This text is the opening passage of the Sumerian literary composition known as **"The Song of the Hoe"** (Sumerian: *Ál*), a creation myth that recounts how the god Enki invented the hoe to relieve the lesser gods of their exhausting labor. The transliteration you provided matches standard academic editions (e.g., ETCSL c.5.5.4; Miguel Civil, *The Farmer's Instructions*, 1994).

Below is a line-by-line scholarly English translation, followed by brief notes on damaged signs and key terms.

### **English Translation**
1. In those remote days, when heaven and earth were fashioned,  
2. In those remote nights, when heaven and earth were fashioned,  
3. In those remote years, when the fates were decreed,  
4. When the Anuna gods were born,  
5. When Ama-dinanna assumed supreme authority,  
6. When Ama-dinanna was apportioned heaven and earth,  
7. When Ama-dinanna […] multiplied and gave birth,  
8. When the gods of the rations were bound to their banquet halls,  
9. All the gods stood idle at their labors, while the lesser gods carried the earth-baskets,  
10. The gods of the waterways were digging, heaping its soil at Ḫarali,  
11. The gods of the clay were kneading it, giving it breath and decreeing its destiny,  
12. In those days, the broad-wisdomed, the life-force of all the gods, ever-present,  
13. Enki, in the deep Abzu, the boundary waters, a place no god could behold, whose interior was unseen,  
14. Lay resting in his bed, and sleep would not depart from him,  
15. The gods wept and called out, full of sorrow and lamentation,
